extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and scientists interested in induction and the logic of empirical generalizations
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and cautionary rules for forming, assessing, and applying inductive generalizations (both universal and approximate), with attention to when generalizations amount to empirical laws and how to measure their strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between coexistence generalizations and causal (succession) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of coexistence (properties that objects possess together) lack a universal axiom analogous to the law of causation for sequences of phenomena and therefore admit different methods and degrees of certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elimination methods (Method of Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations) that work for causal succession are inapplicable to many coexistence questions; treat coexistence uniformities as empirical and avoid assuming they follow the same rigorous inductive procedures as causal laws. Example: 'All crows are black' is a coexistence generalization and cannot be handled by elimination in the same way as cause-effect inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate ultimate properties from properties dependent on causes
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property is an ultimate property of a Kind, it is not due to external causes; if it varies among individuals of the same Kind it is likely an effect of causation and thus an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a trait (e.g., color) is intrinsic to the Kind or variable due to external causes. Variability within organized beings strongly suggests derivative (caused) properties; for simple substances or definite compounds constancy of properties argues for ultimate properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty measured by improbability of undiscovered exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of certainty for a generalization from past observation is the improbability that an exception, if existent, could have remained unobserved up to now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the question as how likely it is that counterexamples have escaped notice (e.g., white crows undetected vs discovery of a new Kind). Use this assessment to judge how far to extend a generalization beyond observed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: If property is effect of causes then empirical-law status and scope follow
rubrics_metrics.description: When the uniformity (e.g., all observed crows being black) results from causes present throughout the observational limits, the generalization can be received as an empirical law within those limits and extended to adjacent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for common causes across observed instances; if causes plausibly exist everywhere in the observational domain, the generalization is stronger. If not, hold it as more provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of universal law of coexistence requires enumeration of sub-kinds before broad generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal propositions about properties of superior Kinds, unless grounded in causation, ought to be based on separate examination of every known inferior Kind (infimæ species) included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer a property for a whole higher Kind from partial sampling of its sub-kinds; exhaustive or representative examination of each sub-kind is required when no causal link is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher generality increases evidential weight (but remains empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: As empirical generalizations become more general (apply to broader Kinds), they typically become more certain because they show resilience across many combinations of circumstances; yet they remain empirical rather than necessary laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broad empirical regularities as nearer to laws of nature, requiring stronger counter-evidence to overturn, but remain open to anomalies and new Kinds that may invalidate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations (Most A are B) are distinct and primarily provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Many inductive truths are admitted as non-universal: 'Most A are B' statements are common and valuable, especially as steps toward universal truths, but have limited deductive utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize their role as pragmatic guides rather than firm scientific conclusions; they are often useful when universal laws are unavailable, but more for practical decision-making than for deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of probability for approximate generalizations depends on observed proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of inferring that an individual A is B from 'Most A are B' is proportional to the ratio of affirmative to negative instances in nature (e.g., 9/10 gives a 1/10 chance of error for an uncharacterized individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When numerical precision is obtainable, assign corresponding probabilistic confidence, but only within the limits of time, place, and circumstances encompassed by the observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When causes or distinguishing marks are known, verify approximate generalizations indirectly
rubrics_metrics.description: If the causes or distinguishing properties that separate As that are B from those that are not are known, one can check these causes/marks in the individual case rather than rely on the coarse generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer examining causal indicators or marks (e.g., school attendance to infer literacy) when feasible, since this yields stronger, case-specific evidence than applying genus-level averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averages apply only to average, uncharacterized cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical averages (general proportions) are applicable only to cases known to be average; applying a genus-level average to a particular known sub-species or to an instance influenced by special circumstances is likely misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using general averages for decisions about particular individuals or non-average cases (insurance-lives example). Instead refine by subclass-specific data or the individual's circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine approximate generalizations carefully: addition vs deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When using multiple approximate generalizations together, they may combine in two ways: 'addition' (independent supports where joint probability rises) or 'ratiocination/deduction' (chain where probability can fall below each component).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the premises are independent (two witnesses' independent testimony) or chained/hearsay (one witness reporting another). Use probability theory to compute joint support in independent cases; beware self-infirmative chains that reduce overall reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical generalizations without causal grounding must be confined to observed limits and ready to be revised
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of coexistence, whether ultimate truths or derivative, are to be ranked among empirical laws and are only justifiable within the limits of observation; they should be promptly revised upon credible counter-evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit claims to the temporal, spatial, and circumstantial domain of observation; give full credence to credible reports of exceptions, especially when plausible that previous observation could have missed them (example: credible witness seeing a white crow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple enumeration is the fallback when elimination cannot be applied
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where elimination (identifying invariable antecedents) is inapplicable, we must rely on simple enumeration of instances (per enumerationem simplicem) and assess strength by the absence of contradictory instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that such enumerative induction provides only empirical, context-limited assurance; its strength depends on the extent and variety of the observations and is weaker than causally grounded induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized beings' variability implies derivative, cause-dependent properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Because organized (living) beings are highly modifiable and influenced by many causes, variability of properties among individuals and over time indicates those properties are likely derivative rather than ultimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating generalizations about organisms, assume dependence on causes and seek causal explanations rather than treating traits as intrinsic Kinds' properties.
